cl_nic_vapes_harms.q: Is it safe to use a vape to quit smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_harms.short: Nobody can say for sure. In quit-smoking trials, serious health problems were about as common with a nicotine vape as with patches or gum: 7 against 6 in 100.
cl_nic_vapes_harms.but: Serious problems were few, and the trials lasted about 2 years at most. That's too few and too short to show rare or later harms.
how: A review of trials, searched up to January 2026, looked at adults who smoked and were given regulated nicotine vapes to help them stop. They were followed for 1 week to about 2 years. The review says this doesn't apply to people who never smoked, and that cannabis or illicit vapes may carry different harms.

Serious health problems: 7 in 100 with a vape against 6 in 100 with patches, gum or similar (10 trials, 4,045 people), and 2 in 100 in both groups against a vape without nicotine (11 trials, 1,786 people). Side effects of any kind were about as common too: 39 against 41 in 100, and 46 against 46.

Against counselling only or no help, the evidence is weaker. Serious problems: 3 in 100 in both groups (18 trials, 5,032 people; 10 of them recorded none). Side effects of any kind: 52 in 100 with a vape against 43, though the range includes no difference.

Some trials found more throat or mouth irritation, cough or dry mouth with vapes; others found fewer breathing symptoms. One found more nausea with patches, gum or similar. No trial against those was paid for by the tobacco or vape industry; one or two in each of the others were, and leaving them out didn't change what the review concluded.
cl_nic_vapes_harms.rate: Chance decided who got a vape, but serious problems were too few to rule out a small difference, and side-effect results varied between trials. The comparison with counselling or no help is weaker still.

cl_nic_pouches_stopping.q: Do nicotine pouches help people stop smoking?
cl_nic_pouches_stopping.short: Nobody knows yet. Four small trials, with 284 people over 8 weeks at most, couldn't tell whether pouches help people quit or cut down.
cl_nic_pouches_stopping.but: Three of the four trials took people who weren't planning to quit. None compared pouches with patches or gum for quitting.
how: A review of trials, searched up to January 2025, found only four small ones in adults who smoked: 284 people, followed for 7 days to 8 weeks. Ten more trials are under way.

In one trial of 45 people, 1 of 18 given pouches had quit at week 8. That compares with 0 of 9 who kept smoking as usual and 4 of 18 given a nicotine vape. None of these gaps, or those in cigarettes a day, can be told from chance, and the trial had serious design flaws.
No serious health problems were recorded in the three trials that reported them, over 1 to 8 weeks. Other side effects were reported in different ways and were mostly mild or uncommon.

A trial paid for by a tobacco company tested 53 people after about a week. Those on pouches had less carbon monoxide in blood, and less of a tobacco chemical in urine, than those who kept smoking. No other trial measured these.
cl_nic_pouches_stopping.rate: Four tiny trials of 8 weeks at most, mostly in people not trying to quit, and people knew what they were given. So few people quit that any gap could be chance.

cl_nic_vapes_exposure.q: Does vaping put fewer toxic chemicals in your body than smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_exposure.short: Yes, much less of most. But not clearly less nicotine. In a US survey, people who only vaped had about 98% less of one cancer-linked chemical than people who only smoked.
cl_nic_vapes_exposure.but: These are chemical levels, not illness. And people who both vaped and smoked didn't have the lower levels.
how: A US survey in 2013 and 2014 compared 247 adults who only vaped (93 in 100 had smoked before) with 2,411 who only smoked. Those who only vaped had about 98% less of a cancer-linked tobacco chemical in their urine and 30% to 97% less of some others. Most metals and a few other chemicals didn't differ.

Short studies where people switched to vaping found the same for carbon monoxide and most other chemicals. So did reviews for the UK in 2022 and by a US expert panel in 2018. Some of those studies were paid for by tobacco companies, but the survey, paid for with public money, agrees.

In the survey, nicotine was 93% lower, but only 59 in 100 of those who only vaped said their vapes had nicotine. In the UK review's pooled studies, nicotine didn't clearly differ. The US panel judged that adults used to vaping take in about as much as from cigarettes.

People who only vaped still had more of some chemicals than people who used no tobacco or nicotine. In the survey, people who both vaped and smoked had as much as people who only smoked, or more, at about the same number of cigarettes a day. Most who vaped had smoked for years, and no study looked past about a year.
cl_nic_vapes_exposure.rate: A survey at one point in time and short switching studies, some paid for by tobacco companies, all point the same way. But most people who vaped had smoked before, and these are chemical levels, not illness.

cl_nic_vapes_disease.q: Does vaping cause heart or lung disease?
cl_nic_vapes_disease.short: Nobody can say yet. A big US study found no clear rise in heart disease in people who only vaped, and more lung problems that past smoking may explain.
cl_nic_vapes_disease.but: It's one study, of illnesses people reported themselves, over 4 years at most. Only 41 people who only vaped got heart disease, too few to be sure either way.
how: The study followed about 24,000 US adults for up to 4 years. New heart disease or stroke was reported by 41 of 822 who only vaped, 764 of 14,832 who used neither, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both. The groups differed in age and time followed, so these counts aren't rates.

Allowing for age, health and past smoking, people who only vaped didn't clearly differ from people who used neither, while those who smoked, or smoked and vaped, had about 1.5 times the rate. But the group who used neither included people who had quit smoking, and those who only vaped had smoked more in the past.

In the same study, new lung conditions such as asthma or COPD came to about 2.6 in 100 people a year among those who had ever vaped, against 2.0 among those who never had. Most who vaped had smoked, and without allowing for past smoking the gap looked far bigger. The authors say this can't show that vaping caused it.

Three reviews were done for the US, UK and Australian governments. They found no evidence, or too little, on heart attack, stroke, long-term lung disease or cancer from vaping. The Australian one judged that vapes did cause a lung injury outbreak (EVALI), mostly vapes with THC.
cl_nic_vapes_disease.rate: Two analyses of one US study, based on illnesses people reported, with few heart cases among people who only vaped. Most who vaped had smoked, and nobody was followed past 4 years.

cl_nic_vapes_dependence.q: Is vaping as addictive as smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_dependence.short: Less, it seems, but still common. In a US survey, 77 in 100 adults who only vaped daily said they felt dependent, against 94 in 100 who only smoked daily.
cl_nic_vapes_dependence.but: Nearly all who vaped had smoked before. And the survey is from 2013 to 2014, before disposables and newer liquids were common.
how: A US survey in 2013 and 2014 compared 156 adults who only vaped daily with 3,430 who only smoked daily. Fewer who vaped said they had strong cravings (73 against 87 in 100) or found it hard to go without where it was banned (6 against 29 in 100).

They also waited longer after waking to first use it: about 29 minutes against 20, on average. The question about places where it's banned fits vaping less well. And there's no agreed way to compare the two.

Other US surveys pointed the same way, and so did surveys of young people in England in 2021. There, about half of 16- to 19-year-olds who vaped felt a little or very dependent, against 83 in 100 who smoked. In one web survey, bigger, more advanced vapes and liquids with more nicotine went with higher dependence scores.

A US expert panel judged that vaping can lead to signs of dependence, and, less firmly, that the risk is lower than with smoking. An Australian review was surer of this for people who don't smoke than for those who do. Each survey was a one-time look, and nobody followed people over time.
cl_nic_vapes_dependence.rate: One-time surveys of what people said, with no follow-up. Nearly all who vaped had smoked before, past smoking wasn't allowed for, and the data predate newer vapes like disposables.

cl_nic_vapes_nearby.short: Nobody knows yet. None of the studies we read checked the health of people nearby. Vaping does add nicotine and tiny particles to the air, but less than cigarette smoke.
cl_nic_vapes_nearby.but: The studies were small and short, minutes to hours, mostly from 2014 to 2017. Nobody followed people nearby for weeks or years.
how: In test rooms, homes and a vaping convention, studies found more nicotine and tiny particles in the air when people vaped, a US expert panel says. The more people vaped, the higher the levels. An Australian review found too little proof to say if these levels harm health.

In one home study, 5 people who didn't smoke lived with someone who vaped. Their saliva and urine held more of a nicotine breakdown product than those of people in homes without vaping. A UK review of six studies found no change after short exposures, but rises after long, heavy vaping nearby.

Vaping gave lower levels than smoking in all four studies that compared the two: in one test room, about a tenth of the nicotine and a fifth of the tiny particles. The US panel says nobody knows what that means for health. It adds that children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may be at special risk.

A Dutch team measured the breath of 17 people after one puff, then worked out worst cases on a computer. Safety margins were small for some chemicals, like nicotine in a car, but the team called the effects fairly mild. Nothing was measured in a real room, car or person nearby.
cl_nic_vapes_nearby.rate: Small, short studies of the air and of a few people's body levels, mostly from 2014 to 2017, plus computer models. None of the studies we read measured the health of people nearby.

cl_nic_vapes_relative_risk.q: How much less harmful is vaping than smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_relative_risk.short: Nobody has measured it yet. People who vape take in much less of many smoke chemicals than people who smoke. But the famous claim that it's 95% less harmful is disputed.
cl_nic_vapes_relative_risk.but: No study we read tracked illness or death for years in people who only vape against people who smoke. It all rests on chemical levels, short studies and what experts think.
how: In a UK review, people who vape had much lower levels of many smoke chemicals than people who smoke. Signs of one family of tobacco chemicals were 58% to 94% lower. A US expert panel found that people who fully switched from smoking did better on short-term lung, heart and mouth checks in all but one of 15 studies.

The UK review was done for the government. It says its 2015 figure, that vaping is at least 95% less harmful than smoking, still broadly fits the short and medium term. It now prefers to say vaping carries a small share of smoking's risks, but grants it isn't risk-free, most of all for people who never smoked.

Critics in 2015 and 2020 say the figure came from the views of 12 people at one meeting in 2013, whose own paper admitted a lack of hard evidence. The 2020 critics say vapes have changed too much to rely on it. Still, they grant that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco nitrosamines.

An Australian review says comparing with smoking can't show what vaping does by itself. A 2022 critique says that's the comparison that matters. Against using no nicotine at all, the UK review found harmful exposure the same or higher.
cl_nic_vapes_relative_risk.rate: The sources we read give no long-term counts of illness or death. The figures rest on chemical levels, short studies (many of the chemical ones paid for by tobacco companies) and expert opinion.

cl_nic_exercise_cravings.q: Does a short burst of exercise help with the urge to smoke?
cl_nic_exercise_cravings.short: Right afterwards, it seems to. In 19 trials, people rated their urge about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale after a short walk or bike ride than after sitting still.
cl_nic_exercise_cravings.but: The urge was rated only once, minutes later, and people knew they had exercised. No study here checked whether it helps people quit.
how: A review pooled 19 small trials in adults who smoke. They hadn't smoked for at least 2 hours, weren't using patches, gum or similar, and mostly weren't trying to quit. They did a short bout of exercise, mostly walking or cycling at a moderate pace, or sat quietly instead.

Right afterwards, people rated their urge to smoke about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale. Every trial pointed the same way, but the size ranged from a fraction of a point to more than 4. Tensing muscles while sitting showed among the smallest effects.
The urge was rated only once, right after or 5 minutes later. So these trials can't say how long the drop lasts, or whether it helps people stop or stay stopped.

People knew whether they had exercised, and the review didn't check how well the trials were run. 17 of the 19 trials list at least one of the review's authors. The review used its own institutions' money, and its authors report no tobacco or drug-company ties.
cl_nic_exercise_cravings.rate: 19 trials all point the same way, but people knew they had exercised and rated their own urge, the size varied a lot, and most trials involved the review's own authors.

cl_nic_oral_nrt_withdrawal.q: Does nicotine gum or an inhaler ease the first week of quitting?
cl_nic_oral_nrt_withdrawal.short: For some symptoms, it seems so. In 12 older trials, people on nicotine gum, an inhaler or a tablet were less grumpy in the first week than on a dummy.
cl_nic_oral_nrt_withdrawal.but: The review only counted which trials found a difference, not how big it was. And a drug company paid for it.
how: A 2001 review gathered 12 trials from 1984 to 2000, with 15 to 240 people each. Most had smoked a fair amount or a lot. After stopping, they got nicotine gum (8 trials), an inhaler (3) or a tablet under the tongue (1), or a dummy version (in one trial, low-nicotine gum).

People on nicotine felt less grumpy than on a dummy in all 9 trials that measured it. Overall discomfort was lower in 6 of 7, anxiety in 3 of 4, and low mood in the one trial that checked it. Results were mixed for restlessness, poor focus, sleep problems and hunger.
Cravings were lower in 7 of 11 trials: all 4 trials of the inhaler or tablet, but only 3 of the 7 gum trials.

Trials that didn't report a symptom left blanks, which may hide results that found no difference. Nothing is known past the first week, no lozenge trial was found, and patches and nasal sprays weren't included.
cl_nic_oral_nrt_withdrawal.rate: Old trials where chance decided who got nicotine. But the review counted only which trials found a difference, unreported results may hide ones that found none, and a drug company paid for it.

nicotine.statement: In quit-smoking trials, vapes clearly did more serious harm than patches or gum.
nicotine.why: No clear difference showed up: 7 against 6 in 100 had serious problems. But problems were few, and the trials lasted about 2 years at most, too short to show rare or later harms.

nicotine.statement: Trials show that nicotine pouches help people quit smoking.
nicotine.why: Nobody knows yet: four small trials of 8 weeks at most couldn't tell. Three of them took people who weren't planning to quit.

nicotine.statement: If you vape, you take in as many harmful chemicals as if you smoked.
nicotine.why: Much less of most: in a US survey, about 98% less of one cancer-linked chemical, though nicotine wasn't clearly lower. These are chemical levels, not illness.

nicotine.statement: Vaping as well as smoking cuts the smoke chemicals in your body.
nicotine.why: In a US survey, people who both vaped and smoked had as much as people who only smoked, or more, at about the same number of cigarettes a day.

nicotine.statement: Studies have shown that vaping causes heart disease.
nicotine.why: Nobody can say yet. In a big US study, people who only vaped had no clear rise in heart disease over 4 years at most, but only 41 of them got it: too few to be sure either way.

nicotine.statement: Most adults who vape every day, and don't smoke, say they feel dependent.
nicotine.why: In a US survey, 77 in 100 adults who only vaped daily said so, against 94 in 100 who only smoked daily. The survey is from 2013 to 2014, and nearly all had smoked before.

nicotine.statement: People who vape daily feel just as addicted as people who smoke daily.
nicotine.why: Fewer reported signs of dependence in a US survey: 73 in 100 adults who only vaped daily had strong cravings, against 87 in 100 who only smoked daily. It's what people said, and nearly all who vaped had smoked before.

nicotine.statement: Vaping indoors leaves the air as clean as before.
nicotine.why: Studies found more nicotine and tiny particles in the air, though less than with cigarette smoke. None of the studies we read checked whether that harms people nearby.

nicotine.statement: The famous figure that vaping is 95% less harmful comes from long-term health studies.
nicotine.why: No study we read tracked illness or death for years in people who only vape against people who smoke. Critics say the figure began as the views of 12 people at one meeting in 2013; a UK review says it still broadly fits the short and medium term.

nicotine.statement: In studies, a short walk eased the urge to smoke, compared with sitting still.
nicotine.why: In 19 small trials, the urge was about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale right afterwards. It was rated only minutes later, and people knew they'd exercised.

nicotine.statement: In trials, people on nicotine gum and the like felt less grumpy in their first week off smoking.
nicotine.why: All 9 trials that checked found less grumpiness in the first week than with a dummy version. The review gave no sizes, and a drug company paid for it.
